newsitem.title: USA: Texas, Fla. oppose Prudential class settlement.
newsitem.headline: Texas, Fla. oppose Prudential class settlement.

text.p: Texas and Florida said they formally object to a proposed class action settlement of consumer complaints against Prudential Insurance Co of America.
Massachusetts also said it opposes the proposed class action settlement of deceptive sales practice allegations against Prudential.

"The proposed settlement places an almost impossible burden on consumers who want compensation beyond the token 'basic claim relief' that the class action attorneys worked out with Prudential," Texas Insurance Commisioner Elton Bomer said.
"These consumers have been shortchanged once. They should not be shortchanged again," he said.

Florida officials said they believe the settlement will not adequately compensate policyholders and unfairly requires them to prove they've been deceived into buying life insurance many of them could not afford.
A copy of Florida Insurance Commissioner Bill Nelson's objections will be made available on the Internet.
The proposed settlement calls for Prudential to pay at least $410 million to resolve lawsuits by policyholders who allege they were victims of deceptive sales practices.
About 10.7 million individuals who bought permanent life insurance policies between 1982 and 1995 would be eligible to apply for restitution.
A Prudential spokesman said, "We believe the settlement is fair and equitable to the policyholders, and 45 states agree with us."
California said it expects to make a statement on the class action settlement sometime today.
Virginia said its negotiations with Prudential are continuing and it will not file anything with the court today.
Policyholders must decide by today whether to participate in the class action settlement.
A hearing on the fairness of the settlement is scheduled for January 21 before U.S. District Judge Alfred Wolin in Newark, N.J.

Florida's Nelson last week filed a formal administrative complaint alleging Prudential had obstructed a state probe of the company's sales practices. He said Prudential could lose its license to operate in Florida if it did not provide requested documents.
The company had until December 30 to answer the complaint.

The Texas Insurance Department said it had urged the federal court handling the Prudential case to enforce an Insurance Department subpoena for records of Texas insurance agents who have been targets of at least three sales-related complaints.
The Texas Insurance Department said Prudential had refused to honor the subpoena.
The Massachusetts attorney general's office is to investigate the destruction of documents at a Prudential office in Cambridge earlier this year.
Prudential, which disclosed the document destruction on Monday, called the action deplorable and said it had dismissed the managing director of the office.
Judge Wolin on Wednesday ordered an investigation into the document destruction and asked for a report by December 27.
((-- Patricia Vowinkel 212-859-1716))
